title: Eternity in Their Hearts
subtitle: Ecclesiastes in Poems & Pictures
author: Timothy Holt
beforeYouBegin:
Ecclesiastes begins with a single word said twice over, vanity, a breath, and then looks hard at everything a person might chase: gardens and pools, silver and gold, wisdom itself. In between: the wind going around, rivers running into a sea that is never full, a time to weep and a time to dance, a threefold cord, bread cast on the waters, an almond tree in blossom, and a silver cord and a golden bowl.

This book walks through it in thirty-six short poems, in four parts. Each poem sits beside a picture and under a single line of Scripture. The pictures stay with the things the Preacher noticed—a lamp just blown out, a heap of field stones, a loaf and a cup—and leave the faces to your imagination.

The poems are not the Bible. They are one reader's response to it. Open the book of Ecclesiastes alongside this book, and let the real words have the last word.

parts.title: Under the Sun
parts.epigraph: Vanity of vanities, all is vanity.
parts.lightHint: Near 'the preacher' (Ecclesiastes 1:1) in Part 1: Under the Sun

parts.title: A Time for Everything

parts.lightName: Light of A Time for Everything
parts.lightHint: Near 'a season' (Ecclesiastes 3:1–2) in Part 2: A Time for Everything

parts.lightName: Light of Better Is the End

paintings.title: the preacher
paintings.epigraph: “The words of the Preacher, the son of David, king in Jerusalem”
paintings.poem:
he had everything
a person could want.

gold in the storerooms.
singers in the hall.
a city at his feet.

and one evening
he sat down
and began to write
about why
none of it was enough.

it's an odd way
to begin a book of the Bible.

it may also be
the most honest.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “the preacher” (Ecclesiastes 1:1)—where the poem notes, “it may also be the most honest”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: breath
paintings.epigraph: “all is vanity.”
paintings.poem:
the old word underneath
is closer to breath.

a puff of warm air
on a cold morning.
there, and then not.

that's the house.
that's the harvest.
that's the name
carved over the gate.

he's not saying
nothing matters.

he's saying
nothing lasts
the way you hoped.

so notice it
while it's warm.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “breath” (Ecclesiastes 1:2)—where the poem notes, “so notice it while it's warm”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: the earth remains
paintings.epigraph: “One generation goes, and another generation comes; but the earth remains forever.”
paintings.poem:
someone's grandfather
walked these terraces.
his grandfather
set these stones.

the olive trees
have outlived them all
and look
no older.

the sun comes up, goes down,
and hurries back around.

it was here
before your name.
it will be here
after.

there's a strange comfort
in being small.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “the earth remains” (Ecclesiastes 1:4–5)—where the poem notes, “there's a strange comfort in being small”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: the wind and the sea
paintings.epigraph: “All the rivers run into the sea, yet the sea is not full.”
paintings.poem:
the wind goes south,
turns north,
and comes back
to where it started.

every river empties itself
into the sea,
and the sea is never full.

he watched it
the way you watch
your own life:

all that running.
all that pouring.
and the wide water
still asking.

some hungers
nothing under the sun
was made to fill.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “the wind and the sea” (Ecclesiastes 1:6–7)—where the poem notes, “nothing under the sun was made to fill”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: nothing new
paintings.epigraph: “there is no new thing under the sun.”
paintings.poem:
the potter
thinks he's made
a new kind of jar.

then he digs a garden
and turns up its twin
in pieces,

someone else's hands,
someone else's morning,
long ago.

whatever road
you're on tonight,
someone walked it
before you

and left
a path.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “nothing new” (Ecclesiastes 1:9–10)—where the poem notes, “and left a path”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: chasing after wind
paintings.epigraph: “all is vanity and a chasing after wind.”
paintings.poem:
go out on a windy day
and catch a handful.

close your fist.
open it.
nothing.

he tried it
with wisdom,
with pleasure,
with work,
and told us plainly:

the wind
is not for keeping.

it's for
feeling on your face.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “chasing after wind” (Ecclesiastes 1:14)—where the poem notes, “it's for feeling on your face”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: great works
paintings.epigraph: “I made myself great works. I built myself houses. I planted myself vineyards.”
paintings.poem:
houses.
vineyards.
gardens and parks.
pools to water
a forest of fruit trees.

and the word he keeps using:
myself.
myself.
myself.

then he walked through it all
and looked.

no profit,
he said.
wind.

the finest garden
in Jerusalem,
and the man who planted it
standing in the middle,
hungry.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “great works” (Ecclesiastes 2:4–11)—where the poem notes, “standing in the middle, hungry”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: from the hand of God
paintings.epigraph: “This also I saw, that it is from the hand of God.”
paintings.poem:
after the palace,
after the gold,

here's what he found:

bread.
a cup.
honest work
and the pleasure of it.

nothing better, he says.

not a consolation prize.
a gift.

it comes
from the hand of God,

and you can
hold it
in yours.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “from the hand of God” (Ecclesiastes 2:24)—where the poem notes, “hold it in yours”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: a season
paintings.epigraph: “a time to plant, and a time to pluck up that which is planted”
paintings.poem:
a time to plant.
a time to pull up.

we want
every season
to be spring,
every door
to be opening.

but the field knows.
it rests.
it gives.
it waits under frost
without complaint.

you're not behind.
you're not broken.

you may just be
in a different month
than you wanted.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: In the quiet after the noise, what gentle truth from Ecclesiastes 3:1–2 (“in a different month than you wanted”) is asking for your unhurried attention today?

paintings.title: weep and dance
paintings.epigraph: “a time to weep, and a time to laugh; a time to mourn, and a time to dance”
paintings.poem:
the same hands
that tore a garment
at the graveside

will lift
the drum again
at a wedding.

grief
keeps its own calendar
and won't be hurried.

but he wrote them
on the same line,
weeping and laughing,
mourning and dancing,

as if to say
neither one
gets the last word
forever.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “weep and dance” (Ecclesiastes 3:4)—where the poem notes, “gets the last word forever”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: stones
paintings.epigraph: “a time to cast away stones, and a time to gather stones together”
paintings.poem:
some years
you clear the field.

some years
you build the wall.

both
are the work.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: If you were to set down one stone of remembrance today for how God has helped you thus far (Ecclesiastes 3:5), what would you name it?

paintings.title: tear and sew
paintings.epigraph: “a time to tear, and a time to sew; a time to keep silence, and a time to speak”
paintings.poem:
there's a time
to tear it open
and a time
to stitch it closed.

a time to say
what needs saying.

a time
to sit beside someone
and say
nothing at all.

the hard part
isn't knowing how.

it's knowing
which day
this is.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “tear and sew” (Ecclesiastes 3:7)—where the poem notes, “which day this is”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: eternity in their hearts
paintings.epigraph: “He has also set eternity in their hearts”
paintings.poem:
everything beautiful
in its time, he says.

and then this:
he has set eternity
in our hearts.

that's why
the best day ends
and something in you
says wait.

we are made
for a longer time
than we have,
a larger story
than we can read
end to end.

the ache isn't a flaw.

it's a compass.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: In the quiet after the noise, what gentle truth from Ecclesiastes 3:11 (“it's a compass”) is asking for your unhurried attention today?

paintings.title: no comforter
paintings.epigraph: “the tears of those who were oppressed, and they had no comforter”
paintings.poem:
he doesn't explain it
or make it tidy.

he sees the tears.
he sees the power,
all on one side.

and he writes it down
twice:
they had no comforter.

sometimes
the faithful thing
is to refuse
to look away.

and then,
if you can,
to be the comforter
they didn't have.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “no comforter” (Ecclesiastes 4:1)—where the poem notes, “to be the comforter they didn't have”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: a handful
paintings.epigraph: “Better is a handful, with quietness, than two handfuls with labor and chasing after wind.”
paintings.poem:
one handful
and quiet.

or two handfuls
and no sleep.

he did the math
for you.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “a handful” (Ecclesiastes 4:6)—where the poem notes, “he did the math for you”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: a threefold cord
paintings.epigraph: “a threefold cord is not quickly broken.”
paintings.poem:
two are better than one.

if one falls,
the other lifts him up.

if two lie down
on a cold night,
there's warmth
enough for both.

then he adds
a third strand
and doesn't say
what it is.

many have heard
God in it.

it would be like him
to be the strand
you can't see,
holding.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “a threefold cord” (Ecclesiastes 4:9–12)—where the poem notes, “you can't see, holding”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: let your words be few
paintings.epigraph: “Therefore let your words be few.”
paintings.poem:
God is in heaven.
you are on earth.

so walk in slowly.
listen first.

you don't have to
fill the silence
to be heard.

a few words,
meant,

are better
than a thousand
you'll forget
by noon.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: In the quiet after the noise, what gentle truth from Ecclesiastes 5:1–2 (“you'll forget by noon”) is asking for your unhurried attention today?

paintings.title: sweet sleep
paintings.epigraph: “The sleep of a laboring man is sweet, whether he eats little or much”
paintings.poem:
the laborer
eats his bread, lies down,
and is gone
before the lamp cools.

the rich man
lies awake,
counting.

not every blessing
can be stored.

some come only
at the end
of an honest day.

you can't buy them.
you can only
lie down and receive.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “sweet sleep” (Ecclesiastes 5:12)—where the poem notes, “you can only lie down and receive”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: the house of mourning
paintings.epigraph: “It is better to go to the house of mourning than to go to the house of feasting”
paintings.poem:
the party
tells you
life goes on.

the funeral
tells you
the truth:

it doesn't,
not like this,
not forever.

so go.
sit with them.
bring bread.

you'll come home quieter,
and hold the people
you love
a little longer
at the door.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “the house of mourning” (Ecclesiastes 7:2)—where the poem notes, “a little longer at the door”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: crackling thorns
paintings.epigraph: “For as the crackling of thorns under a pot, so is the laughter of the fool.”
paintings.poem:
loud.
bright.
snapping and popping.

and the water
never boils.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “crackling thorns” (Ecclesiastes 7:6)—where the poem notes, “and the water never boils”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: the former days
paintings.epigraph: “Don’t say, “Why were the former days better than these?””
paintings.poem:
the old days
always look golden
from here.

we forget the hunger,
the fear, the long nights.

it isn't
a wise question,
he says.

not because
the past was bad,

but because
you can't live there.

the only morning
God has given you
is this one.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: What anxious weight can you place into the hands of the One who says, “Be still” and walks beside you in Ecclesiastes 7:10?

paintings.title: side by side
paintings.epigraph: “In the day of prosperity be joyful, and in the day of adversity consider”
paintings.poem:
a good day?
enjoy it.
don't apologize.

a hard day?
sit down with it.
think.

God set them
side by side,
he says,
like two fields
along one road.

you'll walk through both.

and neither one
tells you
the whole story.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “side by side” (Ecclesiastes 7:14)—where the poem notes, “tells you the whole story”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: upright
paintings.epigraph: “God made man upright; but they search for many schemes.”
paintings.poem:
he went looking
for the scheme of things,
the answer
under everything.

all he could say for sure
was this:

we were made
straight.

and we keep
drawing
crooked plans.

the plumb line
still hangs true.

there's still
something to come back to.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “upright” (Ecclesiastes 7:29)—where the poem notes, “there's still something to come back to”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: bread with joy
paintings.epigraph: “eat your bread with joy, and drink your wine with a merry heart; for God has already accepted your works.”
paintings.poem:
go. eat your bread.
drink your wine.

put on something white.
put a little oil
in your hair.

this from the man
who called everything
breath.

he knew
how short it was.

that's why he said
don't waste the table.

God has already
accepted your works.

you can sit down now.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: How has God quietly provided enough for today’s road, and who might you welcome to your table in kindness (Ecclesiastes 9:7–8)?

paintings.title: with your might
paintings.epigraph: “Whatever your hand finds to do, do it with your might”
paintings.poem:
whatever is in front of you,
the board,
the bread,
the child who needs you,

do it with your might.

he's plain about why:
the day is coming
when there's no more work
to do.

not a threat.
an invitation.

you have hands today.
use them like it matters.

it does.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “with your might” (Ecclesiastes 9:10)—where the poem notes, “it does”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: time and chance
paintings.epigraph: “the race is not to the swift, nor the battle to the strong”
paintings.poem:
the fastest runner stumbles.
the strongest loses.
the wisest man in town
goes without bread.

he doesn't pretend
it's fair.

time and chance
happen to them all.

there's a freedom in that:
you were never
the only one
writing your days.

so run anyway.
just hold the finish line
a little looser.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “time and chance” (Ecclesiastes 9:11)—where the poem notes, “just hold the finish line a little looser”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: the poor wise man
paintings.epigraph: “yet no man remembered that same poor man.”
paintings.poem:
a little city.
a few people.
a great king outside the walls.

and one poor man
who knew what to do.

he saved them all.

then everyone
went back to their lives
and forgot him.

the Preacher
never gives his name.

but he wrote it down,
and here we are,

remembering
a man
no one remembered.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “the poor wise man” (Ecclesiastes 9:14–15)—where the poem notes, “a man no one remembered”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: sharpen the edge
paintings.epigraph: “If the ax is blunt, and one doesn’t sharpen the edge, then he must use more strength; but skill brings success.”
paintings.poem:
you can swing harder.

or you can
sit down a minute
and sharpen the edge.

only a fool
calls that
wasted time.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “sharpen the edge” (Ecclesiastes 10:10)—where the poem notes, “calls that wasted time”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: cast your bread
paintings.epigraph: “Cast your bread on the waters; for you shall find it after many days.”
paintings.poem:
let it go.

the kindness
you can't track.
the gift
no one thanked you for.
the seed
you'll never see sprout.

send it out on the water.
don't chase it down the shore.

after many days,
he says,
you'll find it.

he doesn't say where.

he doesn't say
it will look
the way it left.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: How has God quietly provided enough for today’s road, and who might you welcome to your table in kindness (Ecclesiastes 11:1)?

paintings.title: sow in the morning
paintings.epigraph: “In the morning sow your seed, and in the evening don’t withhold your hand”
paintings.poem:
wait for the wind to settle
and you'll never sow.
wait for the perfect sky
and you'll never reap.

you don't know
the way of the wind.
you don't know
how bones grow
in the womb.

you don't know
which seed
will come up.

so sow in the morning.
sow in the evening.

leave the rest
to the one
who does know.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: What single step right in front of you is already lit by His word today, even if the far horizon remains unseen (Ecclesiastes 11:4–6)?

paintings.title: the light is sweet
paintings.epigraph: “Truly the light is sweet, and it is a pleasant thing for the eyes to see the sun.”
paintings.poem:
after all his hard words,
this:

the light is sweet.

it's good
just to see the sun.

he knows
the dark days
will be many.
he says that too.

but he won't let them
spoil the morning.

open the shutters.
sit in it.

it's allowed.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: What single step right in front of you is already lit by His word today, even if the far horizon remains unseen (Ecclesiastes 11:7–8)?

paintings.title: rejoice in your youth
paintings.epigraph: “Rejoice, young man, in your youth, and let your heart cheer you in the days of your youth”
paintings.poem:
run.
laugh.
follow your heart
out into the morning.

he means it.

and in the same breath
he says:
God will bring you
into judgment.

he isn't taking back
the joy.

he's making sure
it's the kind
you'll still be glad of
later.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “rejoice in your youth” (Ecclesiastes 11:9–10)—where the poem notes, “you'll still be glad of later”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: remember
paintings.epigraph: “Remember also your Creator in the days of your youth, before the evil days come”
paintings.poem:
remember him
now,

while the sun
is still bright,
before the clouds
come back after the rain,

while it's easy
to kneel
and easy
to rise.

not because
he'll forget you later.

because you'll want
to know the way home
by heart
before the lights
begin to dim.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “remember” (Ecclesiastes 12:1–2)—where the poem notes, “before the lights begin to dim”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: the almond tree
paintings.epigraph: “the almond tree shall blossom”
paintings.poem:
he paints old age
like a house
going quiet.

the hands tremble.
the grinding stops.
the windows dim.
the doors close to the street.

you wake at the voice of a bird.
the songs grow soft.

and out on the hill
the almond tree
blossoms white.

every house
goes quiet someday.

the tree
still blooms.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “the almond tree” (Ecclesiastes 12:3–5)—where the poem notes, “the tree still blooms”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: the silver cord
paintings.epigraph: “before the silver cord is severed, or the golden bowl is broken”
paintings.poem:
a silver cord.
a golden bowl.
a pitcher at the spring.
a wheel at the cistern.

lovely things, and breakable.

one day the cord lets go,
the bowl falls,
the pitcher breaks,

and the dust goes back
to the earth it came from.

but that isn't
where the sentence ends:

the spirit returns
to God who gave it.

you were lent.
you are expected.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “the silver cord” (Ecclesiastes 12:6–7)—where the poem notes, “you were lent. you are expected”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: the end of the matter
paintings.epigraph: “Fear God and keep his commandments; for this is the whole duty of man.”
paintings.poem:
of making many books,
he says, there is no end.

(this one included.)

and much study
wears you out.

so here is
the end of the matter:

fear God.
keep his commandments.

not a small life.
a whole one.

everything else
is breath.

this
is what breath
is for.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: What anxious weight can you place into the hands of the One who says, “Be still” and walks beside you in Ecclesiastes 12:12–13?
